lines: Every relationship line on one of these diagrams is answering exactly one question.
How many of this thing, for how many of that one.
Three shapes do all the work here: a ring, a dash, and a crow's foot.
Put two of them together on one end of a line, and you get a minimum and a maximum at once.
A dash on both ends of this line. One customer, one card, and neither side gets to skip the other.
A customer can have many orders, but every single order points back to just one customer.
So which table actually stores that connection?
answer: The order table. Each order only ever needs to name one customer, so that fits in a single column.
The customer side would need a column holding a whole list of orders, and an ordinary column just can't do that.

lines: Watch where the key actually sits once you draw it out.
One value per order, pointing at exactly one customer. That is the whole reason it lands here and not there.
Now both ends of the line get a crow's foot.
An order lists many products, and the same product shows up on many different orders.
Neither table can hold that on its own, so a third one shows up.
It carries a key pointing to each side, and together those two keys usually become its own primary key.
Swap just one symbol, from a dash to a ring, and that one end goes from required to optional.
Nothing else about the shape changes. Read it straight off the diagram, never off the relationship's name.
Three paired symbols, the key on the many side, and a third table whenever both sides say many.
Carry that forward, because the next refresher asks a sharper question about these same tables.
